summary: Gives the profile for DCCP Congestion Control ID 3, which uses TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC). It suits senders that want a sending rate comparable to TCP's, possibly with Explicit Congestion Notification, while avoiding abrupt rate changes. It is standards-track and was later updated by several RFCs.

eli5.summary: Another way to share the road: instead of sudden speed jumps, it changes speed smoothly while staying fair to everyone else. Good for calls and streams.

questions: how does tfrc calculate sending rate
subtitle: A smooth, TCP-friendly sending-rate controller for DCCP, driven by receiver reports of loss events.

tldr.problem: Streaming-style applications want a sending rate comparable to TCP's without the abrupt rate cuts of TCP-like congestion control, which halves its rate at each congestion event.
tldr.mechanism: CCID 3 plugs TFRC into DCCP: the receiver reports loss intervals and receive rate roughly once per round-trip time, and the sender limits itself to the rate the TCP throughput equation gives for the measured loss event rate.
tldr.outcome: Senders get a smoother rate than TCP, at the price of reacting more slowly to changes in available bandwidth. RFC 4342 has been updated by RFC 5348, RFC 6323 and RFC 8311.

today: RFC 4342 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5348, RFC 6323 and RFC 8311, so read it together with those updates.

sections.title: What CCID 3 Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4342 is the profile for Congestion Control Identifier 3 (CCID 3) in the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP, RFC 4340). DCCP uses CCIDs to name the congestion control mechanism in use on one half-connection: the application data sent by one endpoint plus the acknowledgements sent back by the other.

CCID 3 uses TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC, RFC 3448). TFRC is receiver-based: the sender's allowed rate is set from the loss event rate, which the receiver typically reports. The result is a rate close to what TCP would get, with fewer abrupt changes.

The RFC says CCID 3 suits flows that prefer a smooth rate, such as streaming media with small or moderate receiver buffering. TCP-like control, such as CCID 2 (RFC 4341), halves its rate on each congestion event and cannot be smooth.

Smoothness has a cost: CCID 3 responds more slowly to bandwidth changes than TCP. Applications that just want to move data as fast as possible should use TCP-like control, and applications that vary packet size rather than packet rate need a new CCID.
sections.eli5: Some programs, like video calls, hate sudden speed changes. This is a way of sharing the network that changes speed gently but still plays fair with others.

sections.title: How the Sender Picks Its Rate
sections.content:
The sender feeds the loss event rate, a round-trip time estimate and the average packet size into the TCP throughput equation from RFC 3448. The result is the fair rate the sender is limited to. The sender starts in slow start, roughly doubling its allowed rate each round-trip time, until the receiver reports a dropped or marked packet.

RFC 3448 starts at one packet per round-trip time. CCID 3 instead allows at least two and at most four packets per round-trip time, following the larger TCP initial windows of RFC 3390. Three or four packets are allowed only when that stays within 4380 bytes per round-trip time.

Two guard rails apply. The allowed rate is at most twice the receive rate the receiver last reported, so after an idle or application-limited period the sender can at most double each round-trip time. And a nofeedback timer, set to at least four round-trip times or twice the packet interval (whichever is larger), halves the rate when no feedback arrives. The rate is never reduced below one packet per 64 seconds.

CCID 3 is meant for applications with a fixed packet size that vary the number of packets per second. A sender MAY average the packet size over recent loss intervals or use the maximum segment size.
sections.eli5: The sender looks at how many of its packets got lost and uses a formula to find a fair speed. If it hears nothing back for a while, it slows down to be safe.

sections.title: A Half-Connection in Practice
sections.content:
The RFC gives an informative walk-through. The sender sends DCCP-Data packets at its allowed rate; each carries a sequence number and a window counter value in the CCVal field. The receiver sends DCCP-Ack packets at least once per round-trip time, unless the sender sends less than one packet per round-trip time. Each ack names the most recent packet received and carries loss-interval feedback.

The sender updates its allowed rate from this feedback, using a loss event rate it calculates from the reported loss intervals (or, if it prefers, the one the receiver reports). It also estimates round-trip times and keeps the nofeedback timer. If that timer expires, the sender halves its rate.

Only acknowledgements that carry valid Loss Intervals, Elapsed Time and Receive Rate options count as feedback packets. The receiver MAY also add options such as Loss Event Rate or Ack Vector, but CCID 3 does not need Ack Vector.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps sending, and the receiver keeps sending back little notes about what got lost. The sender adjusts its speed based on those notes.

sections.title: Options, Features and Loss Intervals
sections.content:
CCID 3 defines three options and one feature. All of its options MUST be ignored on DCCP-Data packets.

  • Receive Rate (194, length 6): bytes per second received since the last acknowledgement. MUST be sent on all required acknowledgements.
  • Loss Event Rate (192, length 6): the inverse of the receiver-computed loss event rate, rounded up, in data packets per loss interval. Before any loss it is 2^32 - 1.
  • Loss Intervals (193, variable): up to 28 loss intervals, newest first, each 9 bytes (Lossless Length, ECN Nonce Echo plus Loss Length, and Data Length). Receivers MUST report at least the latest 9 unless fewer exist.
  • Send Loss Event Rate feature (number 192): lets one end ask the other to send Loss Event Rate options.

A loss interval begins with a lost or ECN-marked data packet, includes at most one round-trip time of further packets that may be lost or marked (the lossy part), and ends with any number of clean data packets (the lossless part). A missing packet only starts a new interval after NDUPACK = 3 later packets arrive.

The 4-bit window counter in CCVal rises by one about every quarter round-trip time. The receiver uses it to decide whether two losses belong to the same loss event, and when to send feedback, without needing its own round-trip time estimate.
sections.eli5: The receiver sends back a list of stretches of good packets between the bad ones, plus how fast data is arriving. That list is all the sender needs to pick a fair speed.

sections.title: ECN and Checking the Receiver
sections.content:
CCID 3 supports Explicit Congestion Notification (RFC 3168). In a typical ECN-capable half-connection the sender uses the ECN Nonce (RFC 3540) on its data packets. The receiver MUST return nonce information in the Loss Intervals option, and any Ack Vector options MUST include the ECN Nonce Sum.

This lets a sender check the receiver. A receiver that hides a lost or marked packet to avoid a rate cut has only a 50% chance of guessing the correct Nonce Echo for each loss interval. The sender can also compare reported loss intervals and any Loss Event Rate option against what it computes from its saved window counters. Differences should not automatically be treated as misbehavior.

Even without ECN, the sender could occasionally skip a packet or send one out of order to catch a receiver misreporting. The RFC notes this is not as robust or non-intrusive as the nonce. The security section defers to RFC 4340 and RFC 3448 for general concerns, including spoofed feedback and incorrect receiver information.
sections.eli5: Because the sender trusts the receiver's notes, it needs a way to catch fibbing. The nonce is like a secret coin-flip tally that is hard to fake.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
Data packets need not carry Timestamp options: the sender can store send times and use the Acknowledgement Number and Elapsed Time on each required ack to compute round-trip time. Alternatively it MAY send Timestamp options and get Timestamp Echo options back.

Rather than a feedback timer, CCID 3 receivers generally use the window counter to decide when to send feedback. The receiver remembers the greatest counter value at its last feedback and sends a new feedback packet when a data packet arrives with a counter at least four higher. A feedback timer can still help in rare cases to prevent an unnecessary halving of the sender's rate.

When Ack Vector or Data Dropped is in use, the sender MUST acknowledge the receiver's acknowledgements about once per round-trip time so the receiver can free state. The receiver decides the sender has gone quiet after T seconds without data, where T is the greater of 0.2 seconds and two round-trip times.
sections.eli5: Instead of using a clock, the receiver counts the sender's ticking counter to know when to send its next note.

sections.title: IANA Considerations and Future Changes
sections.content:
The document defines value 3 in the DCCP CCID namespace and creates three CCID 3-specific registries: Reset Codes, option types and feature numbers, each in the range 128-255. It allocates option types 192-194 and feature number 192. Values 184-190 and 248-254 are permanently reserved for experimental and testing use, and the rest are allocated by Standards Action.

An appendix lists places where TFRC's behavior may not match what DCCP users want, such as the initial rate, an ack for every packet at low rates, the doubling limit and the halving after an idle period. It calls for research before changing them.
sections.eli5: The document reserves number 3 as this method's name tag and sets aside blocks of numbers for its extras.
